stem: At discharge, which action best supports accurate medication information during the transition of care?

options.A: Review the discharge medication information for accuracy and communicate the current medication list to the client and next care setting as applicable.
options.B: Copy the preadmission medication list without accounting for changes made during hospitalization.
options.C: Omit medication review when the admission was uncomplicated.
options.D: Assume medication information does not need to be communicated after discharge orders are written.

rationale: Joint Commission National Performance Goal #14 requires hospitals to maintain and communicate accurate patient medication information. At a transition such as discharge, medication information should reflect the current regimen and be communicated appropriately rather than simply copying an outdated preadmission list. A is correct.
educational_objective: Maintain and communicate accurate medication information during discharge transitions.
source_document_title: National Performance Goal #14: Effectively Managing Medications
source_locator: Standards — hospital maintains and communicates accurate patient medication information
source_claim_supported: Hospitals must maintain and communicate accurate patient medication information as part of medication safety.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — medication reconciliation and transition safety
blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — medication information at transitions

source_original.stem: A nurse is preparing a client for discharge and performs medication reconciliation, and a colleague assumes this just means checking off the pre-admission list without comparing it to what was actually ordered during the stay. This process specifically instead involves:

options.A: Compare the preadmission, inpatient, and discharge medication lists and resolve discrepancies
options.B: Copy the preadmission medication list without comparing inpatient or discharge changes
options.C: Skip medication reconciliation after uncomplicated admissions because discrepancies are rare
options.D: Leave discharge medication reconciliation entirely to pharmacy with no nursing involvement

source_original.rationale: Discharge medication reconciliation involves systematically comparing the client's pre-admission medication list with medications ordered during the hospital stay and the final discharge medication list, to identify and resolve any discrepancies (omissions, duplications, dosing changes) before the client leaves, a critical patient safety process at this vulnerable transition point.
source_original.source_detail: Medication reconciliation at transitions: compare medication information and resolve discrepancies before transition/discharge; current NPSG framework; accessed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Updated the obsolete NPSG framing to the Joint Commission's 2026 National Performance Goal #14 and narrowed the item to the public current standard: maintaining and communicating accurate medication information at transition; reduced difficulty to easy.

audit_findings.currentness: NPG framework effective 2026 replaced the prior hospital NPSG framing used in the source item.
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final wording is limited to the current public standard to maintain and communicate accurate medication information.

distractor_audit.B: Risks inaccurate information after inpatient changes.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: A uniquely meets the current NPG requirement.
audit_findings.cueing: Removed colleague cue and unnecessary role-allocation claim.
audit_findings.blueprint: Medication reconciliation/transition safety fits Safety and Infection Prevention and Control.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked current NPG #14 and 2026 Joint Commission framework; A remains unique.
